newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EP rejects proposal for maximum VAT rate.
newsitem.headline: EP rejects proposal for maximum VAT rate.

text.p: The European Parliament refused on Thursday to endorse European Commission plans to set a maximum VAT rate of 25 percent throughout the European Union from January 1 1997 to December 31 1998.
Given the lack of consensus among the member states, the Commission has delayed plans to introduce a new origin-based VAT system, originally scheduled for January 1997.
In the meantime, it has come up with a proposal aimed at preventing the different national rates of VAT from drifting even further apart - COM(95)731.

The parliament's economic and monetary affairs committee said it made sense to fix a maximum tax rate of 25 percent, alongside the minimum rate of 15 percent currently in force but on the instigation of the Socialist group MEPs voted by 158 to 143 to reject the move.
Although the parliament does not have the power to block the Commission's proposal, today's vote will strengthen the hand of those countries resisting further tax harmonisation.
There were three reasons for rejecting the 25 percent limit, Dutch Socialist Alman Metten told Reuters.

"We are talking about this in the context of moves towards economic and monetary union which forces member states to cut their budgets or raise taxes. VAT is one of the very few areas where the member states have room for manoeuvre so it would be bad to close off that avenue," Metten said.
He pointed out that the VAT rate in Sweden and Denmark was already at 25 percent.
The Commission itself had provided the second argument against setting a ceiling on VAT, Metten explained.
In its 1993 white paper on growth, competitiveness and unemployment, the EU executive recommending shifting taxation away from labour onto other sources.

"If you make an analysis of what other sources there are, you have excise duties and VAT," he said, adding that the Commission had suggested VAT might be a good source in its working document to the informal ECOFIN Council in Verona in March.

The present transitional VAT system, which came into force in 1993, replaced VAT controls and payments at the EU's internal borders with a system obliging importers and exporters to submit regular VAT records to the authorities.
Although national VAT rates differed widely, ranging from 15 percent in Germany to 25 percent in Scandinavia, there was no evidence of this causing major distortions of competition, Metten said.

The Commission's argument for preventing rates drifting further apart was only relevant as a step towards complete harmonisation of VAT and this was not likely to happen before the end of the century, if at all, Metten insisted.
The Socialists' dim view of the prospects for a single EU tax area are shared by the German Christian Democrat rapporteur for the parliament's economic and monetary affairs committee, Werner Langen.

Whilst recommending approval of the Commission's proposal, Langen's report warns: "The Council has hitherto blocked any more extensive harmonisation of taxation policy and will manifestly continue to do so".
